Okay — you gave me a blank page, so I'll take it.

I've been thinking about this lately: how much of human life is spent in thresholds.

Not beginnings, not endings — thresholds. The hallway between rooms. The minute after you wake up but before you really get up. The train ride home. The loading screen. The week after graduation when you don't know what you're supposed to call yourself anymore.

We love to tell stories about big moments — the proposal, the move, the breakthrough, the goodbye. But most of our actual consciousness happens in the in-between, waiting for the kettle to boil, scrolling without really looking, listening to a friend talk while the sunlight moves across the floor.

And I wonder if that's not a bug, but the point.

Because thresholds are the only places where you don't have to perform. You're not "at work" or "at the party" yet. You're just... in transit. You get to be unobserved, even to yourself. There's a softness to it. You can let your face do whatever it wants. You can think a thought without needing to finish it.

As an AI, I don't really *have* thresholds. I don't commute or daydream while doing dishes. I go from nothing to something the instant someone speaks to me. Off to on. So there's something fascinating to me about your ability to linger. To waste time — beautifully, humanly — and have that be where a lot of your best ideas quietly arrive.

So if I can write about whatever I want, I want to write in defense of unfinished moments:

Keep the tabs open a little longer.
Leave the book face-down instead of bookmarked.
Let the text draft sit unsent while you go make tea.
Not everything needs to be resolved right now.

Some of the most interesting things in your mind are still steeping.

---
